title: Physics-Inspired All-Pair Interaction Learning for 3D Dynamics
one_liner: A neural network designed to find how every object in a multi-body system pushes or pulls on every other object, using physics principles to make the learned rules work correctly even on new, unseen systems.
lead: Predicting how a group of objects will move—a person's skeleton, molecules bouncing, or proteins folding—requires knowing not just what forces are there, but which objects are actually interacting with each other. Most recent models try to guess these connections from what they can see in the data, but they miss hidden interactions that matter. PAINET builds all possible object-pair connections into the model from the start, then learns which ones are actually strong. It uses physics-inspired attention (a technique from mathematics that mimics how physical systems minimize energy) to weigh each connection fairly, and ensures the learned rules work the same way no matter how you rotate or move the whole system.

paras: When you watch a pendulum swing, or a protein fold, or a human walk, you are seeing the result of forces—pushes and pulls between the parts. To predict what happens next, you need to know two things: which pairs of objects are actually interacting, and how strong each interaction is.

Current models try to learn this by looking at the data they are given. They might see that one part usually moves with another, or stays close to it, and assume they are interacting. But this fails in three ways: first, they only learn connections they can literally see in the data; second, they miss interactions that happen inside objects and never show up in positions (like the flex of a tendon or the bent angle of a bond); third, when you test the model on a new system—a person of a different height, or a molecule with a different shape—these learned guesses often do not work because the scale or arrangement of the objects is different.

A beginner might try: build a model that takes all the positions, and routes every position through a learned graph that decides which connections exist. This often fails because the graph it learns is brittle—it is tuned to the exact shapes in the training data, not to the underlying physics.

callout.b: The method in one plain sentence.
callout.html: PAINET assumes all object pairs interact, learns which interactions are important through physics-inspired attention (a mathematically grounded scoring mechanism), and enforces rotation/translation symmetry so the learned rules work on any system.

panels.title: 1. The problem: hidden interactions
panels.caption: A system has many objects. Some pairs interact strongly, some weakly, some not at all. You cannot see the weak ones.

panels.title: 2. Old way: guess from the data
panels.caption: Model learns which connections to keep (hot), which to ignore (free). But it overfits to that specific system's exact shape.

panels.title: 3. PAINET: start with all pairs
panels.caption: Instead, assume every pair interacts. Physics-inspired attention scores each pair fairly using an energy principle.

panels.title: 4. Energy scoring: fair weighing
panels.viz_args: Pair score = how much positions change when this pair pulls on that pair
panels.caption: Score each pair by asking: if these two moved, how would it shift the system's total energy?

panels.title: 5. Result: works on new shapes
panels.caption: Learned attention weights transfer to new systems because they follow physics principles, not memorized shapes.

steps.text: Take the raw 3D positions of all objects and turn them into a list of numbers (an embedding).
For each pair of objects, compute an attention score using an energy-inspired formula, measuring how much that pair affects the system's total energy.
Weight each pair's effect on an object's future motion by its attention score, then add all the weighted effects together.
Ensure the learned rules treat rotation, translation, and reflection the same way (SE(3)-equivariance), so a rotated copy of a system predicts the same rotated motion.
Output how each object's position and velocity will change in the next time step.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: Most models learn which object pairs interact by building a flexible graph structure and guessing from the training data. PAINET instead computes an attention score for every pair using a fixed physics-inspired formula. The object being changed is: the mechanism that weighs how much each pair of objects influences the motion of each other.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: pair influence score
hidden.name: pair influence score
paras: The paper measures a quantity called the pair influence score: for each pair of objects (object A and object B), this number says how much A's motion is driven by B, or vice versa. It is based on a principle from physics: if two objects are interacting, then moving one should shift the system's total energy. Pairs that shift more energy are scored higher.

PAINET estimates this score using an attention formula derived from energy function minimization. In other words, it asks: if I nudge object B a tiny amount, how much does the system's total energy change? If the change is big, the pair is scored high; if the change is small, the pair is scored low. This is not guessed from data; it is computed using the current positions and learned features of both objects.

heat.caption: Darker means higher influence score. Highlighted pairs are the strong interactions the model learns to rely on.

reads.html: The influence score measures how much one object's motion depends on the other. A high score means strong interaction; a low score means weak or no interaction.

The paper derives the attention scores using a mathematical formula based on how energy changes when objects move (using calculus concepts from physics), making the weighting grounded in principles rather than learned flexibly from data alone.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The core idea is that objects in physical systems interact according to forces, and forces are tied to energy. If you have an energy function describing the system, you can compute how much each pair contributes by asking: if this pair were removed, would the energy change a lot or a little? Pairs that matter change the energy a lot; pairs that do not matter change it hardly at all.

PAINET builds this principle into the model by using an attention mechanism derived from energy minimization. Instead of asking the model to guess which pairs interact from the data, it uses a fixed, physics-rooted formula to score every pair. This formula does not depend on the specific scale or arrangement of the system you trained on—it depends only on the relative positions and learned features of the objects. So when you test the model on a new system (taller person, different molecule, different protein), the scoring still works because it follows physics, not the memorized layout.

Additionally, PAINET enforces that its learned rules are equivariant to rotation and translation: if you rotate the entire system, the predictions rotate too, and if you shift it, the predictions shift the same way. This is automatic, because the model only uses relative positions and angles between objects, never absolute coordinates. This symmetry constraint makes the learned interactions transfer cleanly to new systems with new scales and orientations.

stages.s: Positions and features of all objects
For each pair, compute relative position and learned feature difference
Apply energy-inspired attention formula to score the pair
Weight each object's future motion by the attention scores of all its pairs
Predicted positions and velocities at the next time step

math.words: For each object i, its predicted future position is the sum over all other objects j of the attention score between i and j, multiplied by the learned interaction effect from j on i, all divided by a sum of attention scores to keep the total reasonable. The attention score is based on a quadratic form of the relative position and features between i and j, using a learned matrix.
math.equation: position_i_next = sum_j [ attention_ij * interaction_effect_ij ] / sum_j [ attention_ij ]; attention_ij = exp( -0.5 * (r_ij^T M r_ij) ); r_ij = (position_j - position_i, feature_j - feature_i)
symbols: predicted position of object i in the next time step
learned importance score between objects i and j (higher means stronger interaction)
the learned change in i's motion caused by j
the relative position and feature difference between objects j and i
a learned positive-definite matrix that weighs different dimensions of the difference
exponential function (makes negative numbers become positive scores between 0 and 1)

worked.title: A tiny worked example with two objects
lines: Object A and Object B: distance between them is 2 units.
Relative vector r_AB = [2, 0, 0] (close on x-axis, far on y and z).
Learned matrix M: emphasizes x differences more (to capture a direct bond). M = diag(4, 0.5, 0.5).
For comparison: if A and B were 10 units apart, energy = 2*4*10 = 80, attention = exp(-40) ≈ 0 (almost no interaction).
Learned effect if nearby: interaction_effect_AB = 0.15 (B pulls A forward a little).
A's motion update from B: 0.00034 * 0.15 ≈ 0.00005 (very small, because they are far).
If they were very close (r_AB = [0.1, 0, 0]): attention = exp(-0.02) ≈ 0.98, update = 0.98 * 0.15 ≈ 0.147 (much bigger).
The exponential ensures nearby pairs have high influence, distant pairs have nearly zero.

math.note: The attention score decays exponentially as objects move apart, because the energy term grows quadratically with distance, so close pairs always dominate the motion updates.

items.b: Scaling to systems with many objects.
items.html: If a system has 1000 objects, computing attention for all pairs means 1,000,000 comparisons. This is expensive because the model must compute an attention score for every pair, and the compute time grows as the square of the number of objects. The paper includes a parallel decoder to speed up when the model answers a new question, but training on very large systems may still be slow because training requires computing all those attention scores many times.

The model learns a weighting table (a table of numbers that says which dimensions of the difference between two objects matter most). This must capture the right physics for each system. If the training data is limited or noisy, this table might learn the wrong principles and fail on new systems anyway.

Enforcing SE(3)-equivariance (rotation, translation, reflection symmetry) is mathematically strict. If the model is not built carefully, it can leak information from absolute positions or orientations, breaking the symmetry and reducing transfer to new systems.

When all three pieces are correct (energy-inspired attention, learned matrix, SE(3)-equivariance), the model's learned interactions transfer cleanly from training systems to new geometries, sizes, and configurations the model has never seen.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple 3D physics simulator: take 5 point masses connected by springs. Train PAINET on one configuration (e.g., the 5 points arranged in a line). Then test it on a completely different configuration (the 5 points arranged in a star, or a circle). Also test on the original configuration with one spring removed or softened. The demo should show: PAINET's predicted positions stay close to ground truth on the new configurations, because its learned attention weights still identify the spring interactions correctly; in contrast, a model that memorizes the interaction graph from training data fails on the new configurations, because it learned the wrong pairs or memorized the exact shape of the original arrangement.
demo.metric_eq: transfer error = average distance error on new configuration / average distance error on training configuration; PAINET should have transfer error < 1.5x, baseline should have transfer error > 3x
demo.closing: The core mechanism: PAINET works on unseen system arrangements because it does not memorize which pairs interact, but learns to score pairs using physics-grounded energy principles that work regardless of shape or scale.
